A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Geminio and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite the expanded and reorganized supplementary material.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-20, and FER, including baseline comparisons, defense evaluations, and supplementary label-inference experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds caption-query evaluation, VLM comparisons, FL-round experiments, and reconstruction-quality analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Figure 2 add an explicit deployment branch: non-victim clients train a benign model, and only their gradients enter its aggregation while the victim receives malicious parameters. This is a limited extension of the described procedure; the VLM-guided loss and soft-label equations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The datasets remain ImageNet, CIFAR-20, FER, and the existing auxiliary sources. V2 modestly extends scenario coverage through caption-defined ImageNet retrieval and explicit background-object targeting in Appendix F. The added CIFAR-20 illustrations and 128-image examples do not introduce new datasets or previously untested batch-size coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 7 adds HFGradInv, previously cited but not evaluated there, alongside retained DLG and InvertingGrad comparisons, each with and without Geminio. The five targeted-attack comparators in Figure 5 and five supplementary label-inference methods remain.

E3.justification: The stated default reconstruction algorithm changes from InvertingGrad to HFGradInv. Appendix F introduces caption-generated queries for randomly selected images, alternative VLM configurations, random versus current-global-model initialization across FL rounds, and a fixed batch of 256 with varying matched-sample counts. The existing CIFAR-20 evaluation and 0.90 gradient-similarity threshold remain.

E4.justification: Appendix F substantially expands analysis of query complexity, VLM choice, attack timing and initialization, reconstruction sensitivity to matched-sample count, and background-object targeting. These investigate generalization and failure conditions beyond v1's retained auxiliary-data, architecture, defense, label-inference, and batch-size analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing averaging practices remain, and the additional experiments continue to report point estimates without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds caption-query, FL-round, matched-count, and VLM results, including SigLIP's 69.54% versus CLIP's 68.13% F1. Figure 7 adds HFGradInv LPIPS values of 0.66 alone and 0.19 with Geminio and revises existing scores. It also corrects Figure 8's prose to match the unchanged bars. Updated reconstructions use a revised default algorithm, preventing a simple same-setting improvement claim.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the gradient-dominance reasoning remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the existing training mathematics; no new theorem, proof, or substantive formal derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim attacks at any FL round while preserving normal model utility. The central contributions—natural-language targeted inversion, compatibility with reconstruction algorithms, and resistance to existing defenses—retain their original scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands applicability explanations and limitations: auxiliary data must represent queried features, advanced VLMs better handle complex queries, and reconstruction deteriorates beyond roughly 16 matches with the tested backend. It also argues that client selection can undermine model-history inspection and explains utility preservation through separate benign aggregation.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 explicitly documents initialization and training steps. The appendix adds HFGradInv integration information and identifies BLIP-based query generation. The repository link, CLIP checkpoint, hardware, optimizer, and reported feature-extraction and poisoning times are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds a specific CI-Net scalability comparison and references supporting captioning, auxiliary data, and larger-batch training, while removing several general gradient-inversion citations. Its central positioning as the first natural-language interface for semantically targeted GIAs remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and portions of the introduction, threat model, and method explanation are rewritten. The appendix is reorganized around new pseudocode and extended analyses, with affiliation and acknowledgement edits. Much of the original experimental narrative and overall section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redrawn, Figure 4 expands from two to three dataset panels, and Figure 7 gains a third reconstruction method. Main-text plots are resized and rearranged, and the short final appendix example panel is replaced by extensive new plots and reconstruction displays in Figures 26–34.

improvement.justification: V1's quantitative validation of language-guided targeting largely relies on CIFAR subclass names. V2 addresses this important gap with caption-based ImageNet evaluation and substantially clarifies applicability through attack-timing tests and an explicit matched-sample capacity limit. These additions strengthen the central claim and expose a meaningful failure boundary; pseudocode also improves inspectability. The stronger utility-preservation claim still lacks a direct utility comparison, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the claim-relevant validation and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.
